summary: Leaving the temple for the last time, Jesus foretells its destruction and His own return, and calls His disciples to watch, endure and be ready.
key_insight: The disciples asked about stones and timing. Jesus answered with a command He repeats again and again: take heed, watch. The discourse is less a timetable than a call to readiness.
story: Late in His last week, Jesus left the temple for the last time. As they walked out, one of His disciples said, “Teacher, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!” Jesus answered, “Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone shall be left upon another, that shall not be thrown down.” {Mk}

Later He sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, and Peter, James, John and Andrew asked Him privately, {Mk} “Tell us, when will these things be? And what will be the sign of Your coming, and of the end of the age?” {Mt}

Jesus began, “Take heed that no one deceives you.” Many would come in His name. There would be wars and rumors of wars, famines and earthquakes, but these were only the beginning of sorrows. His followers would be hated and handed over to councils and kings, yet the gospel of the kingdom would be preached in all the world as a witness to all the nations. “But he who endures to the end shall be saved.” {Mt}

Then He gave them a sign. When they saw the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel, standing where it ought not, {Mk} when they saw Jerusalem surrounded by armies, {Lk} those in Judea must flee to the mountains without going back for anything. Great distress would fall on the land, and Jerusalem would be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. {Lk}

He warned them not to chase rumors of false christs, for His coming would be as plain as lightning flashing from east to west. {Mt} After the tribulation of those days, the sun would be darkened and the powers of the heavens shaken, and “they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.” He would send His angels with a great sound of a trumpet to gather His elect from the four winds. {Mt}

“Now learn this parable from the fig tree,” He said. When its branch becomes tender and puts out leaves, summer is near. “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will by no means pass away.” Yet the day and hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. {Mk}

So He called them to watch. It would be as in the days of Noah, when people went on eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the flood came. {Mt} It would be like a man who went to a far country, gave each servant his work, and told the doorkeeper to watch. {Mk} “Watch therefore, and pray always.” {Lk} Matthew records more pictures still: the faithful and wise servant, the ten virgins, the talents, and the Son of Man on His glorious throne, separating the nations as a shepherd divides the sheep from the goats. {Mt}
“And what I say to you, I say to all: Watch!” {Mk}

Through those last days Jesus taught in the temple by day, and at night He went out and stayed on the mountain called Olivet. Early in the morning all the people came to Him in the temple to hear Him. {Lk}
differences: Matthew’s question adds “the sign of Your coming, and of the end of the age.” Mark and Luke ask only when the temple will fall and what the sign will be.
Where Matthew and Mark speak of “the abomination of desolation,” Luke says “Jerusalem surrounded by armies.”
Mark says that no one knows the day or hour, “nor the Son, but only the Father.” In the NKJV, Matthew reads “but My Father only” (some manuscripts of Matthew include “nor the Son”).
Matthew is by far the longest. He adds Noah, the faithful servant and the three teachings of chapter 25: the ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and the goats.

Luke alone speaks of “the times of the Gentiles” and warns against hearts weighed down with carousing, drunkenness and the cares of this life. He alone closes with Jesus teaching in the temple by day and lodging on Olivet by night.

fit.question: Matthew and Mark say the sign is “the abomination of desolation.” Luke says it is “Jerusalem surrounded by armies.” Did Jesus give two different signs?

points.label: Luke explains Daniel’s phrase
points.text: Luke wrote for Gentile readers like Theophilus, who would not know the phrase from Daniel. He tells them what it would look like in practice: armies surrounding the city that would defile the holy place.

points.label: One event, two descriptions
points.text: Mark even signals that the phrase needs explaining: “let the reader understand” (Mark 13:14). Luke does the explaining.

fit.note: Luke translates a Jewish phrase into plain terms; the sign is the same.
fit.short: Luke explains Daniel’s phrase for Gentile readers: the sign would be Jerusalem surrounded by armies.

fit.question: Jesus said, “This generation will by no means pass away till all these things take place” (Matthew 24:34). Was He wrong about the timing of His coming?

points.label: The temple’s fall
points.text: Many hold that “all these things” means the destruction of the temple, which came in AD 70, within one generation, just as Jesus said. His coming in glory, whose day no one knows, is a separate and later event.

points.label: Near and far together
points.text: Others see the fall of Jerusalem as a preview of the final day, the way the prophets often saw a near event and a far one together, like two mountain peaks that look like one from a distance.

points.label: A kind of people
points.text: Others read “generation” as a race or kind of people that will remain until the end.

fit.note: Faithful believers read the timing differently, but all agree on what Jesus stressed: His words will not fail, His coming is certain, and His people must be ready.
fit.short: Many see the temple’s fall in AD 70, within a generation; others see a near event previewing the final one. Views differ.

scene.label: Herod’s temple
scene.text: Herod the Great rebuilt and enlarged the temple, and the work was still going on in Jesus’ day (John 2:20). Some of its stones were enormous, and the whole complex gleamed with white stone and gold.

scene.label: AD 70
scene.text: About forty years later, Roman armies under Titus surrounded Jerusalem, burned the temple and pulled it down. Josephus, an eyewitness, recorded the siege. Early church tradition says Christians remembered Jesus’ warning and fled across the Jordan to Pella.

scene.label: The Mount of Olives
scene.text: This ridge east of the city faces the temple across the Kidron Valley. Zechariah 14:4 speaks of the Lord standing on it in the day of His coming. Luke says Jesus spent His nights there during this last week (21:37); Bethany, where He lodged earlier in the week (Matthew 21:17), lies on its eastern slope.

scene.label: Daniel’s phrase
scene.text: “The abomination of desolation” comes from Daniel 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11. Every Jew remembered how Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple in 167 BC.

scene.label: The fig tree
scene.text: Most trees in Israel keep their leaves all year. The fig loses its leaves in winter, so new leaves are a clear sign that summer is near.

witnesses.matthew: Gives the fullest account and joins the question about the temple to the question about Jesus’ coming and the end of the age. He adds Noah, the faithful servant and the teachings of chapter 25, so the King’s last public teaching ends with the King on His throne, judging the nations.
witnesses.mark: Is compact and urgent. “Take heed” and “watch” run through the chapter, and the final word is addressed to every reader: “Watch!” Mark’s aside, “let the reader understand,” speaks straight to the church.
witnesses.luke: Separates the fall of Jerusalem clearly: armies, captivity and “the times of the Gentiles.” He sets the teaching in the temple courts and stresses prayer and a heart that is not weighed down, so believers can stand before the Son of Man. He ends with a picture of those last days: Jesus in the temple by day, on Olivet by night, and the people coming early in the morning to hear Him.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the Lord of history. He sees the temple’s fall forty years ahead and His own return in glory, and He calls Himself the Son of Man who will gather His people.
seeing.living: Jesus gives no dates; He gives a way to live. Do not be deceived or alarmed. Endure, keep doing the work He gave you, and pray. Readiness looks like faithfulness on ordinary days.
seeing.ponder: If the Master came at an hour you do not expect, what would He find you doing? Is your heart weighed down, or watching?

preaching.big_idea: We do not know the hour, so we watch every hour.
preaching.watch_for: Mark 13 repeats its warning like a drumbeat: “take heed” or “watch” (vv. 5, 9, 23, 33, 35, 37). The main application is readiness, not a timeline.
